title: A Birthday: date and placing
short: Written in 1857, first printed in Macmillan's Magazine (April 1861) and collected in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), it is one of Rossetti's rare poems of pure joy.
body: Rossetti's manuscripts date the poem to 1857; it first appeared in Macmillan's Magazine in April 1861 and was collected in her first commercial volume, Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862). In a body of work dominated by renunciation, grief and waiting, this is an outburst of fulfilment, which has made its occasion a puzzle. No biographical lover has been identified with certainty. The poem's two stanzas move from nature (similes of bird, tree, shell) to art (commands to build a ceremonial dais), both expressing the inexpressible joy announced in the last line.

anchor: My heart is like an apple-tree
title: Anaphora and similes
short: Three similes beginning 'My heart is like' build to a fourth line that surpasses them all: 'gladder than all these'.
body: The first stanza is a series of parallel similes in loose iambic tetrameter, with few rhymes ('shoot' and 'fruit'; then 'tree', 'sea', 'these' and 'me', so that the closing lines gather into one rhyme), closing with 'My heart is gladder than all these / Because my love is come to me'. The structure echoes biblical parallelism, especially the Song of Songs, and the method of exceeding one's own comparisons is a traditional sign of overwhelming emotion. Each simile adds a dimension: song (bird), fruitfulness (tree), colour and calm (shell).

title: a watered shoot
short: The bird nests in a young branch nourished by water, an image of flourishing that recalls the righteous man of Psalm 1.
body: A 'shoot' is a young branch. The phrase recalls Psalm 1:3, the blessed man 'like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season', and Isaiah 58:11, 'thou shalt be like a watered garden'. The bird is secure and the place fertile. The 'singing bird' also echoes the Song of Songs 2:12, 'the time of the singing of birds is come', in the passage where the beloved calls 'Rise up, my love'.

title: apple-tree with thickset fruit
short: An apple-tree loaded with dense fruit: the Song of Songs compares the beloved to an apple-tree among the trees of the wood.
body: 'As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons' (Song of Solomon 2:3). 'Thickset' means closely packed. The apple is also the fruit of Eden and of temptation, which Rossetti explored in 'Goblin Market' in the same volume, but here fruit means plenty and ripeness rather than danger. The bent boughs suggest a heart heavy with gladness.

anchor: That paddles in a halcyon sea
title: rainbow shell; halcyon sea
short: A shell with rainbow sheen floats in a 'halcyon' (calm) sea, named from the kingfisher of Greek myth who calmed the winter waves.
body: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 11) Alcyone and her drowned husband Ceyx are turned into kingfishers (Greek alkyon), and for seven winter days the sea is calm while they nest, the 'halcyon days'. 'Rainbow shell' suggests mother-of-pearl, or perhaps a nautilus, whose shell was believed to 'paddle' or sail on the surface. The word 'paddles' is playful, almost childlike. The rainbow also recalls the covenant of peace after the Flood (Genesis 9:13).

title: dais
short: A 'dais' is a raised platform for a throne or seat of honour; the second stanza commands a ceremonial setting.
body: The second stanza turns from similes to imperatives addressed to unnamed craftsmen: 'Raise', 'Hang', 'Carve', 'Work'. The dais of 'silk and down' (soft feathers) is a throne, a bridal bed or a canopied seat, at once royal and soft. The scene evokes medieval romance and Pre-Raphaelite decoration; Rossetti's brother Dante Gabriel was painting such rich interiors in the 1850s. The imperatives make the speaker a queen or bride giving orders for her own festival.

title: vair; purple dyes
short: 'Vair' is a costly medieval fur (squirrel, blue-grey and white); purple was the dye of kings.
body: Vair (from Latin varius, variegated) was the fur of a squirrel with grey back and white belly, used for lining royal and noble garments, and in heraldry a pattern of alternating blue and white shapes. Purple, made from the murex shellfish of Tyre, was the imperial colour. The vocabulary of a heraldic, royal pageant is one of the poem's ways of treating the beloved's coming as a coronation or a wedding feast.

anchor: Carve it in doves, and pomegranates
title: doves and pomegranates
short: Doves and pomegranates are emblems of love and fertility in the Song of Songs and of the priestly robe in Exodus.
body: In the Song of Songs the beloved is 'my dove' (2:14; 5:2) and her temples are 'like a piece of a pomegranate' (4:3); the lovers' garden has 'an orchard of pomegranates' (4:13). Pomegranates were embroidered on the hem of the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:33-34) and carved on the pillars of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:18). In Christian iconography, the pomegranate, with its many seeds, signifies resurrection and the church. The dove is the Holy Spirit, and in classical art the bird of Venus.

sources.cite: Christina Rossetti, The Complete Poems, text by R. W. Crump, notes and introduction by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin Classics, 2001), notes

anchor: And peacocks with a hundred eyes
title: peacocks with a hundred eyes
short: The 'eyes' of the peacock's tail recall the hundred eyes of Argus, set in Juno's peacock in Ovid.
body: When Mercury killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus, Juno set his eyes in the tail of her bird, the peacock (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.720-723). In early Christian art the peacock, whose flesh was believed incorruptible, is a symbol of immortality and resurrection. Rossetti's details thus combine luxurious ornament with a possible sacred meaning, a doubleness that matters for the reading of the whole poem.

title: fleurs-de-lys
short: The stylised lily of French royal heraldry, also associated with the Virgin Mary.
body: The fleur-de-lis (lily-flower) was the emblem of the French monarchy; the lily is also the flower of the Annunciation and of the Virgin's purity, as in Dante Gabriel Rossetti's painting Ecce Ancilla Domini (1849-50), for which Christina modelled. 'Gold and silver grapes' recall the vine of Christ ('I am the true vine', John 15:1) and the Eucharist, but also simple abundance. The stanza is thick with images that can be read either as courtly splendour or as liturgical symbolism.

title: 'the birthday of my life'
greek: Lat. dies natalis, 'birthday' (of a saint's entry into heaven)
short: The beloved's arrival is a new birth; critics debate whether the 'love' is a human lover or Christ.
body: The phrase means the day on which her true life begins. Readers who take the poem as secular see a joyful erotic lyric about a lover's coming. Others, noting Rossetti's devout Anglo-Catholicism and the poem's imagery from the Song of Songs (traditionally read as Christ's love for the soul or the church), hear a spiritual rebirth, or even death: in Christian tradition a saint's death-day is their dies natalis, birthday into heaven. The richness of the second stanza fits a heavenly marriage as well as an earthly one. The poem itself does not decide.

anchor: my love is come to me
title: 'my love is come to me': the refrain
short: Each stanza ends with almost the same line, the old perfect form 'is come' stressing arrival as a completed fact.
body: 'Is come' (instead of 'has come') is an archaic perfect, familiar from the KJV ('the time of the singing of birds is come', Song of Solomon 2:12) and from Advent and Christmas texts. The refrain gives the poem the shape of a song. In the second stanza 'Because' introduces the reason for all the ceremonial building. The poem has been set to music many times.
